title: The odds of an early bell

data.source: Cramer (1938), Onsager and Machlup (1953), Freidlin and Wentzell (1970), Schroedinger (1915); cited from memory. Closed form, plus one seeded simulation of 60000 paths.

prediction: With weak noise of strength D the chance of a cut by time t, or of none by time t, is exp(-(a - v t)^2/(4 D t)) to leading order: early cuts cost three times the exponent of equally late ones at half and half again the mean time, and with no drive the exponent is R6's least dissipation divided by 4 kT.
baseline: Large deviations: Cramer (1938); Freidlin and Wentzell (1970); the Onsager-Machlup action (1953); the exact first-passage law (Schroedinger 1915). Decoy: a symmetric bell curve.
relation: R4's two-sided bound is the zero-noise limit of the theorem; R6's bound is its exponent
status_line: CRR here is: a special case of large-deviation theory (R4's bounds are its zero-noise limit and R6's bound is its exponent); the odds of an early or late cut come from the theorem, not from CRR.
why: R4 (Phoenix status ASSUMPTION) bounds the duration of an occasion when there is no noise. With weak noise those bounds are broken with a chance that large-deviation theory gives and R1 to R6 do not; the measured exponents approach the theory's as the noise shrinks. R6's inequality (status RESULT, 'existing thermodynamic-length mathematics') is the same Cauchy-Schwarz step that gives the cheapest path, so its bound over 4 kT is the exponent for an undriven half-turn.
